The most commonly recommended stretch for tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is the **wrist extensor stretch**:

1. Straighten your arm in front of you, palm facing down.
2. Let your wrist drop so your fingers point at the floor.
3. With your other hand, gently press the back of that hand toward you until you feel a mild stretch along the top of your forearm.
4. Hold for 15–30 seconds, repeat 3 times, a few times a day.

Only take it to a mild stretch, never to pain. A closed fist makes it stronger if you need more.

**Stretching usually isn't the best fix on its own, though.** The best evidence for tennis elbow is on **eccentric loading**, which strengthens the tendon:

- **Eccentric wrist extension:** Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge, palm down, holding a light weight (0.5–1 kg, or a can of beans). Use your other hand to lift the wrist up. Then lower it slowly on its own over about 3–5 seconds. Do 3 sets of 10–15, once or twice a day.
- **Tyler twist:** This uses a flexible rubber bar (a Theraband FlexBar). Studies have found it works well, and physios often recommend it.
- **Isometric holds:** Push the back of your hand up against a fixed surface for 30–45 seconds without moving it. This helps when the elbow is too irritable for other exercises.

Some mild discomfort during the loading exercises is normal. Pain that's sharp or worse the next day means you should lighten the load.

**See a physio or doctor** if you have numbness or tingling, it isn't improving after 6–8 weeks, or you can't grip things properly. Symptoms usually improve over weeks to months, so keep at it.

Here's how Portugal taxes new residents, based on what I know up to mid-2026. Rules change every year in the budget, so check the current figures with a Portuguese accountant (*contabilista certificado*).

**When you'd become tax resident**
- You're resident if you spend more than 183 days in Portugal in any 12-month period, or if you have a home there that you intend to keep as your usual residence.
- Once resident, Portugal taxes your income from anywhere in the world. A tax treaty with your current country decides which country gets to tax what, and stops you paying twice on the same income.
- Porto and Lisbon are taxed the same way, because income tax is national. Only a few smaller items vary by city (see "Other things to know").

**Income tax (IRS) on salary or self-employment**
- Rates are progressive, from about 12–13% on the lowest band up to 48% on income above roughly €83k.
- An extra "solidarity" charge applies at the top: 2.5% on income over €80k and 5% on income over €250k.
- Social security is also due:
  - Employees pay 11% and the employer adds about 23.75%.
  - Self-employed people pay 21.4%, calculated on 70% of their income.

**Special regimes that could lower your bill a lot**
- **NHR (Non-Habitual Resident) is closed to new applicants.** Anything you've read about a 10% tax on pensions or broad exemptions for foreign income no longer applies to newcomers.
- **IFICI ("NHR 2.0") replaced it.** It lasts 10 years:
  - Qualifying Portuguese work income is taxed at a flat 20%.
  - Most foreign income is exempt, but not pensions or income from blacklisted jurisdictions.
  - The catch is that your work has to qualify. That mainly means tech and startups, research and higher education, or highly qualified roles at certain eligible companies.
  - You can't have been a Portuguese tax resident in the previous 5 years.
- **IRS Jovem** applies if you're under 35. Part of your work income is exempt for up to 10 years:
  - 100% in year 1
  - 75% in years 2–4
  - 50% in years 5–7
  - 25% in years 8–10
  - The exemption is capped at roughly €28–29k a year.

**Investments**
- Dividends, interest and capital gains are generally taxed at a flat 28%. You can choose to add them to your other income and pay the progressive rates instead, which helps if your income is low.
- Crypto held for more than 365 days is generally tax-free. Crypto held for less is taxed at 28%.
- There's no wealth tax.
- Inheritances and gifts between spouses, children and parents are exempt, apart from a small stamp duty in some cases.

**Other things to know**
- Porto sets its own annual property tax (IMI) rate, somewhere between 0.3% and 0.45% of the property's official tax value. It also decides whether to refund residents part of the 5% share of income tax that goes to the city.
- If you're leaving a country that has an exit tax on unrealised gains or on pension transfers, check that before you move.

# The Bandeja

Marco had hit the shot ten thousand times. Maybe more. The bandeja, the flat overhead you slice back deep so it dies in the corner, was the first thing his coach in Valencia taught him and the last thing he'd expect to go wrong.

It was the second set of the club final, 5–4, and the ball came high off the back glass. He set his feet, turned his shoulder and brought the racket through. Something in his wrist went *click*, a small dry sound like a knuckle cracking, and then came a heat that ran up his forearm to the elbow.

The ball went into the net.

"Unlucky," said Javi, his partner, already walking back to position.

Marco flexed his fingers. They worked, but the heat stayed. He served the next point and felt it again, a thin line of pain on the pinky side of the wrist, where the bones meet the forearm.

They lost the set 7–5. He told Javi he was tired and let him think that.

---

The physio was called Inés. She pressed two fingers into the soft hollow below his little finger and he nearly came off the bench.

"TFCC," she said. "Triangular fibrocartilage complex. Very common in padel. It's all that wrist snap on the overheads, and the glass makes you play late."

"How long?"

"Six weeks in a brace if you're good. Longer if you're not."

"The league starts in four."

Inés looked at him the way people look at a dog that has just put its head in a fence. "Then you'll watch the first two matches."

---

The brace was black and made him look like he was halfway through turning into a robot. He couldn't open jars. He couldn't grip a steering wheel properly. The worst part was going to the club anyway, because he didn't know what else to do with his Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and sitting behind the glass watching other people play.

At first it was torture. He watched Javi play with a substitute, a tall kid called Rubén who hit everything hard and flat, and he mouthed corrections nobody could hear.

By the third week he had noticed something. From outside the court, the game looked slower. He could see where the gaps would open before they did. He could see that Rubén always drifted to the middle after a lob, that the opponents on court four telegraphed every chiquita by dropping their shoulder, and that Javi, his partner of six years, hung back at the net whenever Marco was in trouble. He had never known that. Javi had been covering for him the whole time.

He started taking notes on his phone, awkwardly, left-handed.

---

In the fifth week Inés let him take the brace off for ten minutes and squeeze a foam ball.

"Good," she said. "When you go back, and you *will* go back, stop flicking the wrist on the bandeja. Let the shoulder do it. The wrist is a hinge, not an engine."

He thought about that all the way home. A hinge, not an engine.

---

His first match back was a Thursday in late October, under the floodlights. His wrist was taped and he was nervous in a way he hadn't been since he was a teenager.

At 3–3 in the first set the ball came high off the back glass, the same shot as before. He felt the old instinct to snap it.

Instead he turned his shoulder, kept his wrist quiet and let his whole body carry the racket through. The ball went out low and flat, kissed the side glass and died in the corner.

Nobody moved for it.

"That's new," said Javi.

Marco grinned and flexed his fingers. There was no heat and no click.

"Had some time to think," he said.

The **wrist extensor stretch** is the go-to stretch for tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis):

1. Straighten your affected arm out in front of you, palm facing down.
2. With your other hand, gently bend the wrist down so your fingers point toward the floor.
3. Stop at a mild, comfortable pull along the top of your forearm, not pain.
4. Hold for 15–30 seconds and repeat 3–5 times, a few times a day.

To stretch a bit further, make a loose fist before you bend the wrist, or turn your hand slightly so the pinky side rotates outward.

**Stretching alone usually isn't enough.** The approach with the best evidence is **eccentric strengthening**, especially the **Tyler twist** with a FlexBar, or wrist extensor lowers:

- Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge, palm down, holding a light weight (0.5–1 kg or a water bottle).
- Use your other hand to help lift the wrist up.
- Lower it **slowly (3–5 seconds)** using only the affected arm.
- Do 3 sets of 10–15 once or twice a day. Some discomfort is okay, but sharp pain isn't.

**Also helpful:**
- Cut back on whatever triggers it, like gripping, mouse use or backhands. You don't need to fully rest the arm.
- Wear a counterforce strap just below the elbow during activity.
- Be patient. It often takes 6–12 weeks to improve noticeably.

**See a doctor or physio if you have** numbness or tingling, swelling, pain after an injury or fall, or no improvement after 6–8 weeks.

# The Glass Wall

Mateo heard it before he felt it: a small, dry click, like a twig breaking under snow.

It was 5–5 in the third set of the club final. Under the lights, the ball had come off the back glass at a strange angle, low and spinning away. He'd twisted to reach it with a *bandeja* he had hit ten thousand times. The racket met the ball, and the ball floated over the net and died in the far corner. The small crowd along the fence cheered. His partner, Álvaro, shouted his name.

Mateo stood very still, watching his right hand like it belonged to someone else.

"You okay?" Álvaro jogged over, still grinning.

"Fine." He switched the racket to his left hand. Something warm and electric was pulsing just below his thumb. "Let's finish it."

They lost the next four points. He couldn't grip the handle properly, so his volleys came off the frame and his smashes landed in the net. The other team, two brothers in their fifties who had been playing together since before padel came to Spain's coastal towns, were too polite to celebrate much. One of them came around the net and looked at Mateo's wrist, which had started to swell.

"Scaphoid," the older brother said quietly. "I did mine in '98. Don't be stupid about it."

---

Mateo was stupid about it for three days.

He iced it. He wrapped it in tape. On the fourth morning he tried to lift a coffee cup, set it down again very carefully, and drove to the hospital with one hand.

The doctor put the X-ray up on the lightbox and tapped a thin grey line in a bone the size of a cashew. "Eight weeks in a cast. Maybe twelve. This bone has a poor blood supply. It heals slowly, if you let it."

"And if I don't let it?"

The doctor looked at him over her glasses. "Then you'll be asking me that question again in a year, with a much worse answer."

---

The first two weeks were the hardest. He drove past the club on his way to work and kept his eyes on the road. He muted the group chat after Álvaro started posting videos of new partners, then felt ashamed and unmuted it. At night the cast itched in places he couldn't reach, and he lay awake replaying the point: the angle off the glass, the twist, the click.

In the third week, Álvaro showed up at his door with two coffees and a folding chair.

"Come watch," he said.

"I don't want to watch."

"You're not watching for fun. You're coaching. I'm playing with Inés from the Tuesday group, and she keeps drifting to the middle on lobs. You see that stuff better than me."

So Mateo went. He sat on the folding chair behind the back glass with his cast resting on his knee. For the first set he said nothing. By the second set he was standing with his face almost against the wall, calling out *"Stay wide! Wait for it off the glass, don't chase it!"* Inés looked back at him, annoyed, and then stayed wide and won the point.

He had spent ten years inside that glass box and never really seen it from outside. From behind the wall the whole geometry was visible: how the ball rose and dropped off the corners, the gaps that opened when both players moved forward too early, how the brothers always stood a half-step deeper than everyone else. It wasn't luck or age that made them good. They were patient.

---

The cast came off on a Thursday in late autumn. His wrist was pale and thin, and it barely bent. The physiotherapist gave him a rubber ball to squeeze and a list of exercises that felt insulting in their smallness: *rotate, flex, hold, release.*

He did them all anyway, every morning and every night, the way he had once drilled volleys.

In February he held a racket again. In March he hit soft balls with Álvaro, both of them standing at the net and saying nothing, just feeling the rhythm come back. In April he played his first real match. He lost it, and he didn't care.

---

The next club final came around in June. Mateo and Inés reached the last game against, inevitably, the two brothers.

At deuce, the ball came off the back glass at a strange angle, low and spinning away.

Mateo didn't twist. He took one step back and waited. He let the ball come to him off the second wall, the way he'd watched it do a hundred times from a folding chair, and he lifted a slow, easy lob over both brothers into the corner.

The older brother watched it land, then turned and gave him a small nod.

"Better," he said. "Much better."

Mateo flexed his wrist once, the way the physiotherapist had taught him, and walked back to the baseline to serve.

The most common stretch for tennis elbow is the **wrist extensor stretch**:

1. Straighten your arm in front of you, palm facing down.
2. With your other hand, gently bend the wrist down so your fingers point to the floor.
3. Stop at a mild pull along the top of your forearm. It shouldn't hurt.
4. Hold for 20–30 seconds and repeat 3 times. Do this a few times a day.

**Stretching alone usually isn't enough.** Tennis elbow is a tendon overload problem, and tendons recover best when you gradually load them. The exercises with the strongest evidence are:

- **Eccentric wrist extension:** Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge, palm down, holding a light weight (0.5–1 kg, or a can of soup). Use your other hand to lift the weight up, then lower it slowly with the sore arm over about 3–4 seconds. Do 3 sets of 15 once a day. Some discomfort is fine, but it should settle by the next day.
- **Isometric holds:** Keep the same position, but hold the wrist still against resistance for 30–45 seconds. This is useful when the elbow is too irritable for movement.
- **Tyler twist:** This uses a FlexBar (a rubber resistance bar). There's good evidence for it, and a physio can show you the technique quickly.

**Also helpful:**
- For a while, cut back on whatever sets it off, such as gripping, a mouse or your racquet.
- A counterforce brace worn just below the elbow can help some people.
- Improvement usually takes 6–12 weeks of steady work.

**See a doctor or physio if** you have numbness or tingling, the elbow is swollen, the pain followed an injury, you can't straighten your arm, or it isn't getting better after a couple of months.

**When Portugal starts taxing you**
- You become tax-resident if you spend more than 183 days a year there, or if you have a home there on 31 December that you clearly use as your main residence.
- From then on, Portugal taxes your worldwide income. Double-tax treaties usually stop the same income being taxed twice, but your current country may still tax you in your first year, or charge an exit tax.

**Main rates**
- **Income tax (IRS):** progressive, from about 12.5% up to 48%, with the top rate starting around €80k. On top of that there's a solidarity surcharge of 2.5% above €80k and 5% above €250k.
- **Social security:**
  - Employees pay 11% and employers pay about 23.75%.
  - Self-employed people pay 21.4% on 70% of their income.
- **Self-employed "simplified regime":** for most professional services, only 75% of your gross income is taxed.
- **Investments:** dividends, interest and capital gains are taxed at a flat 28%. Crypto held for more than a year is generally exempt.
- **Property:**
  - Buying: transfer tax (IMT) of up to about 7.5%, plus stamp duty.
  - Owning: yearly municipal property tax (IMI) of 0.3–0.45% of the property's tax value, set by each town. Porto's rate is near the low end.
- **Inheritance and gifts:** exempt between spouses, children and parents. Otherwise 10% stamp duty.
- **Wealth tax:** none, except an extra property tax (AIMI) on property worth more than €600k.

**Special regimes that could lower your bill**
- **NHR is closed:** the old Non-Habitual Resident regime stopped taking new applicants in 2024.
- **IFICI (sometimes called "NHR 2.0"):**
  - Income from qualifying work in Portugal is taxed at a flat 20% for 10 years. Qualifying work is mainly tech, research, startups and some highly qualified jobs.
  - Most foreign income is exempt, but pensions are not.

- **IRS Jovem (under 35):**
  - Part of your work income is tax-free for up to 10 years: 100% in year 1, then 75%, 50% and 25%.

# The Bandeja

Mateo had hit the shot ten thousand times. That was the stupid part.

It was the third set on a Thursday night at the club in Poblenou. The floodlights buzzed. Rafa and old Iñaki were up 5–4 across the net, and Iñaki had just floated a lob so high it seemed to hang in the damp October air. Mateo backpedalled, turned his shoulder, and set up for the bandeja: the flat, sliced overhead that keeps you in control of the net without trying to end the point. It was his shot. People at the club called him *el Bandejas*, half as a compliment and half to tease him for never trying anything else.

He misjudged it by half a step. The ball dropped closer to the glass than he expected, so he reached, and at the moment of contact he snapped his wrist to save the angle.

He felt the crack in his forearm before he heard it, a hot white line from the base of his thumb to his elbow. The ball hit the net and dropped. His racket clattered onto the artificial grass.

"Mate?" His partner Lucía was already walking over. "You okay?"

"Fine," he said, the way men say *fine* when they are clearly not. He picked up the racket with his left hand. His right hand would not close around the grip. His fingers trembled like they belonged to someone else.

---

The doctor at the mutua was young and brisk. She turned the X-ray toward him as if showing off a holiday photo.

"No fracture. But you've irritated the TFCC, the cartilage on the pinky side of the wrist. And you have tendinitis here," she said, tapping the screen, "which I'd guess has been building for months."

Mateo thought about the mornings when opening a jar hurt, and the ibuprofen he had started keeping in his padel bag the way other people kept sweatbands.

"How long?"

"Six weeks of rest, then physio. Maybe eight before you play again."

"Eight *weeks*?" The club tournament was in five. He and Lucía had been seeded second.

The doctor shrugged. "Or you can play in five and be out for a year. Your wrist, your choice."

---

The first week was the worst. He wore the brace to work, and everyone asked about it, so he had to repeat the story: *I snapped my wrist on a bandeja.* Nobody outside padel knew what a bandeja was, so he started saying *I hurt it playing tennis*. That felt like a small betrayal.

In the second week he went to the club anyway and sat on the bench behind the glass to watch Lucía play with a substitute, a tall kid named Dani who smashed everything as hard as he could. They lost 6–2, 6–3. Afterward Lucía sat next to him, sweating and annoyed.

"He doesn't know how to wait," she said. "Every ball is a winner in his head."

"He's twenty," said Mateo.

"You were never like that."

"No," he said. "I was worse. I just hid it better."

She looked at him, and he surprised himself by continuing. "That shot on Thursday. I didn't need to save it. I could have let it go past me, played it off the glass, and reset. I just didn't want to look like I'd misread it."

Lucía laughed. "So you broke your wrist out of vanity."

"It's not broken."

"Your *pride* is broken."

---

Physio started in week six. The physiotherapist, Marta, had forearms like a rower's and no patience for his impatience. She gave him a rubber bar to twist, a two-kilo dumbbell, and a list of exercises so boring he wanted to cry.

"Your wrist was doing the work your legs and shoulder should do," she told him. "You get lazy with your feet, you arrive late, and the wrist rescues you. Rescue a hundred times and eventually the rescuer quits."

So he relearned the bandeja from the ground up. He practised in his living room with a broom handle, without a ball, working on footwork. He took three small steps back, turned side-on, kept the elbow high and the wrist firm and *quiet*, and let the shoulder carry the swing. His downstairs neighbour complained about the shuffling at night.

---

He missed the tournament. Lucía played it with Dani, and they reached the quarterfinals, which was better than anyone expected. Mateo watched from the bench with his brace on the last Saturday he needed it, and when Dani hit a bandeja instead of trying to smash a lob, Mateo stood up and clapped louder than was reasonable.

"Did you tell him to do that?" Lucía asked after the match.

"I might have mentioned it."

---

He came back in week nine, on a cold Tuesday in December. For the first twenty minutes his wrist was fine, but his head wasn't. Every overhead made him flinch.

Then Iñaki, naturally, put up another lob, high and floating, dropping toward the back glass.

Mateo felt the old urge to reach and snap his wrist. He didn't give in to it. He let the ball drop, turned, and let it bounce off the glass. Then he played a soft, boring, perfectly placed lob right back over Iñaki's head.

Iñaki scrambled and missed.

"Look at that," Iñaki panted. "El Bandejas learned a second shot."

Mateo flexed his right hand under the lights. There was no pain, just a faint reminder that it was there.

"Took me eight weeks," he said, walking back to the service line. "Worth it."
